text:
Gloria Fuertes was born in Madrid
at the age of two days,
for my mother's labor was so difficult
she nearly died giving me life.
At three I could already read,
and at six I could already do my chores.
I was good and thin,
tall and somewhat sickly.
At nine a cart ran into me,
and at fourteen the war caught me;
at fifteen my mother died—she left when I needed her most.
I learned to bargain in the shops
and go to villages for carrots.
Around then I began to fall in love
—I will not name names—;
thanks to that I endured
my youth in the neighborhood.
I wanted to go to war to stop it,
but they stopped me halfway there.
Then I got an office job,
where I work as if I were stupid
—but God and the office boy know I am not.
I write at night
and often go to the countryside.
All my family died years ago,
and I am lonelier than myself.
I have published verses in every calendar,
I write for a children's newspaper,
and I want to buy on installments a real flower
like the ones Pemán sometimes receives.
